hops.title: Why your fingers are not webbed like a duck's
hops.text: Spread the fingers of one hand. Early in human development, hands and feet start as little paddles, and apoptosis helps clear away the tissue between the growing fingers and toes. Ducks keep that tissue. Their embryos make a protein called Gremlin in the webbing between their toes, and Gremlin blocks signaling proteins called BMPs that help drive the dying there. When researchers added Gremlin between the developing toes of chick embryos, fewer cells died there, and a web of tissue could be left joining the toes. The gaps between your fingers are a record of cells that died on schedule.

sources.citation: Hernández-Martínez R & Covarrubias L, Dev. Growth Differ. 53:245–258 (2011), PMID 21338350.
Merino R et al., Development 126:5515–5522 (1999), PMID 10556075.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A student on a park bench spreading five fingers while looking at a mallard duck lifting its webbed orange foot.
image.caption: Apoptosis cleared the tissue between your fingers; duck embryos make Gremlin, a death-signal blocker, in the webs they keep.

hops.title: Why a leukemia drug was designed to spare platelets
hops.text: Blood platelets have no nucleus, yet they carry the apoptosis machinery. Bcl-xL keeps them alive by holding Bak in check, and platelets from mice lacking Bak live longer than normal. That mattered for cancer medicine. Navitoclax, which blocks both Bcl-2 and Bcl-xL, was active against some blood cancers but sharply lowered platelet counts because blocking Bcl-xL made platelets die early. Chemists reworked it into venetoclax, which targets Bcl-2 far more strongly and spared human platelets in lab tests. Within a day of their first venetoclax dose, three patients with hard-to-treat chronic lymphocytic leukemia had blood-test changes indicating tumor lysis, a potentially dangerous result of rapid cancer-cell breakdown.

sources.citation: Souers AJ et al., Nat. Med. 19:202–208 (2013), PMID 23291630.
U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Medical Review for Venclexta (venetoclax), NDA 208573 (2016).

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A small glass hourglass with trickling sand resting beside a single smooth tablet and a brass magnifying glass on a wooden bench.
image.caption: Bcl-xL helps keep platelets alive, so chemists designed venetoclax to target Bcl-2 and largely spare Bcl-xL.

hops.afterHeading: The first brake: from a lost signal to cytochrome c
hops.title: The sucrose clue that caught cytochrome c
hops.text: In 1996, Xiaodong Wang's group at Emory University made an extract from growing cells in which they could trigger key steps of apoptosis in a test tube. When they fractionated it to find a protein the death program required, it turned out to be cytochrome c, the electron carrier that normally works inside mitochondria. Wang later recalled that most people, his own group included, first feared it was a test-tube artifact. One clue came from plain sugar. Including sucrose to stabilize mitochondria while making the extract weakened the activity, which pointed to cytochrome c leaking out of mitochondria in their original prep. Dying cells, they found, release it too.

sources.citation: Liu X, Kim CN, Yang J, Jemmerson R & Wang X, Cell 86:147–157 (1996), PMID 8689682.
Zagorski N, Profile of Xiaodong Wang, Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A. 103:7–9 (2006), PMCID PMC1324996.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A biochemistry bench with a glass tube of pinkish-red liquid beside a small dish of white sugar crystals and a glass mortar and pestle.
image.caption: Keeping mitochondria intact with sucrose weakened the test-tube death reaction, pointing to leaked cytochrome c.
